prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Today outside your prison I stand and rattle my walking stick: Prisoners, listen; you have relatives outside. And there are thousands of ways to escape. Years ago I bent my skill to keep my cell locked, had chains smuggled to me in pies, and shouted my plans to jailers; but always new plans occured to me, or the new heavy locks bent hinges off, or some stupid jailer would forget and leave the keys. Inside, I dreamed of constellations— those feeding creatures outlined by stars, their skeletons a darkness between jewels, heroes that exist only where they are not. Thus freedom always came nibbling my thought, just as—often, in light, on the open hills— you can pass an antelope and not know and look back, and then—even before you see— there is something wrong about the grass. And then you see. That’s the way everything in the world is waiting. Now—these few more words, and then I’m gone: Tell everyone just to remember their names, and remind others, later, when we find each other. Tell the little ones to cry and then go to sleep, curled up where they can. And if any of us get lost, if any of us cannot come all the way— remember: there will come a time when all we have said and all we have hoped will be all right. There will be that form in the grass.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Today, Prisoners, And

outputs.L1:
Today, outside your prison, I stand and rattle my walking stick: Prisoners, listen; you have relatives outside, and there are thousands of ways to escape.

Years ago, I bent my skill to keeping my cell locked, had chains smuggled to me in pies, and shouted my plans to the jailers. But new plans always occurred to me; the new, heavy locks bent the hinges off; or some foolish jailer would forget and leave the keys.

Inside, I dreamed of constellations—those feeding creatures outlined by stars, their skeletons a darkness between jewels; heroes that exist only where they are not. Thus, freedom always came nibbling at my thoughts, just as—often, in the light, on the open hills—you can pass an antelope without knowing it, then look back, and, even before you see, sense that there is something wrong with the grass. And then you see.

That is how everything in the world is waiting.

Now, these few more words, and then I am gone: Tell everyone simply to remember their names, and remind others later, when we find one another. Tell the little ones to cry and then go to sleep, curled up wherever they can. And if any of us get lost, if any of us cannot come all the way, remember: there will come a time when all we have said and all we have hoped will be all right.

There will be that form in the grass.
outputs.L2:
I am standing beyond the walls of your prison today, striking my cane against the ground to get your attention. Hear me, inmates: people who belong to you are still out here, and escape can be found by countless routes.

Long ago, I used all my ingenuity to make sure my own cell remained sealed. I arranged for chains to be hidden inside pastries and delivered to me, and I announced every scheme within earshot of the guards. Yet another possibility would always arise. Sometimes the weight of a newly installed lock tore the hinges loose; sometimes a foolish guard simply walked away and forgot the keys.

While confined, I imagined the constellations: star-drawn animals that seem to feed in the sky, their bones formed by the blackness separating bright gems, and legendary figures whose shapes appear only in the empty spaces. In this way, the idea of liberty kept chewing at my mind. It was like walking across bright, exposed hills past an antelope without realizing it was there. You turn around, sensing—before you actually spot the animal—that the grass is somehow altered. Then, suddenly, you recognize its shape.

Everything on earth waits to be discovered in just that manner.

I have only a little more to say before I leave. Tell everyone to hold on to their own names. Ask them to help others remember theirs when, someday, we meet again. Tell the children they may weep, then let them sleep tucked into whatever shelter they can find.

And should some of us disappear, or fail to complete the journey, keep this in mind: a day will arrive when every word we have spoken and every hope we have carried will be made right. The hidden outline will finally emerge from the grass.
outputs.L3:
The speaker urges the prisoners to remember that they are not alone. Beyond the walls of their confinement, they have allies who stand with them, and there remain countless paths toward freedom, even if those paths are not yet visible. He admits that he once tried to protect and preserve the very conditions that kept him confined, yet freedom continued to enter his thoughts and shape his circumstances despite his resistance.

Freedom is described as a quiet, hidden presence. It may go unnoticed at first, revealing itself only through a subtle change—a moment when someone recognizes that the world is no longer quite as it was. The prisoners must therefore remain attentive and hopeful. They are called upon to remember who they truly are, to strengthen one another, and to comfort those who are frightened or vulnerable until the time comes when they can all be reunited.

Finally, the speaker acknowledges that not everyone may survive or reach freedom together. Even so, he expresses faith that their words, hopes, and aspirations will endure. If some are lost along the way, what they stood for will remain, carried forward by others until their longed-for future is finally realized.
outputs.L4:
To those who remain behind walls, I speak as one who once counted the same bars and listened for the same footsteps in the corridor. I tried to make my captivity certain and complete. I sealed the cracks through which daylight entered, turned my face from every open door, and trained myself not to dream of roads, fields, or distant voices. I thought that if I could extinguish hope, confinement would become easier to endure.

But freedom would not remain hidden. At night, the constellations appeared beyond the narrow window, arranging themselves into maps no guard could erase. Even in darkness, they spoke of distances that could be crossed and of a world larger than the cell. In the yard, small animals concealed beneath stones or in the grass would suddenly stir and reveal themselves. Their quick movements reminded me that life survives in secret places, waiting for the right moment to emerge.

So I ask you not to believe that the walls contain everything. Remember those who have left, and know that we remember you. Recognize one another in the darkness: the frightened, the forgotten, the wounded, and those who can no longer speak for themselves. Let each person’s courage shelter another person’s weakness.

Hope may seem invisible, but it is not absent. It moves like a hidden creature and shines like a star obscured by cloud. Hold fast until the signs of liberation can no longer be denied, until the lost are found, the vulnerable are protected, and the freedom you have imagined finally stands before you. Then the desires you have guarded in silence will come into the light and be fulfilled.
outputs.L5:
### Prisoners and Society Today

Today, prisoners face many challenges beyond the loss of freedom. They may experience isolation, limited educational opportunities, mental health difficulties, and uncertainty about life after release. Although prisons are intended to protect society and hold people accountable, they should also support rehabilitation.

Education, vocational training, counseling, and family contact can help prisoners prepare for a more stable future. When former prisoners can find work and housing, they are less likely to reoffend. A fair justice system must therefore balance punishment and public safety with dignity, responsibility, and the possibility of change.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical prose poem in the voice of a former prisoner addressing those still confined, using escape, constellations, and an unseen antelope in the grass as metaphors for hope.
counterfactuals.output:
Brothers, sisters, I speak to you from the other side of the wall, though some nights the wall still rises in my sleep.

Do not believe the sky belongs to the guards. Above the yard, beyond the wire’s black stitching, the constellations keep their contraband fire. I used to name them exits. I used to climb them rung by rung with my eyes, until my body remembered there were distances no lock could measure.

Escape began before the gate opened. It began as a small refusal: the heart would not wear a number. It began in the crack beneath the door, where morning laid one thin blade of gold. I hid that light inside me. I sharpened it against despair.

Listen: beyond the fences there is grass moving in the dark. You may see only the trembling stems, the moonlight parting and closing, but somewhere within them an antelope passes—unseen, swift, alive. Hope is like that. You do not need to see its body to know it is running.

I cannot promise when your doors will open. I can only tell you that iron is not eternal, that walls mistake stillness for surrender, and that even caged breath rehearses the wind.

Keep one star unnamed. Keep one path unguarded in your mind. When the night leans close, hear the hidden antelope lifting its delicate feet through the grass.

It is going somewhere.

So are you.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an inspirational monologue that begins outside a prison and assures the prisoners that freedom is always finding a way to reach them.
counterfactuals.output:
I’m standing outside these walls tonight, where the road is open and the wind moves without permission. I can see the watchtowers, the locked gates, the narrow windows—and I know some of you have begun to believe the whole world has become this place.

But listen to me.

Freedom has never depended on an unlocked door.

It enters in a letter folded beneath a pillow. It slips through the bars as morning light. It rises in the memory of a voice that still calls you by your name, not your number. It lives in every book you open, every truth you speak, every kindness you refuse to let this place take from you.

Walls can interrupt a journey, but they cannot erase its destination.

Even now, freedom is looking for you. It is crossing miles in the hearts of people who have not forgotten. It is moving through courtrooms, classrooms, prayers, protests, and promises. It is growing quietly in the choices you make when no one is watching—in the moment you forgive yourself, in the moment you begin again, in the moment you decide that your worst day will not become your final identity.

You may not be able to reach the horizon tonight, but the horizon is still reaching toward you.

So guard the part of yourself no lock can touch. Feed it with hope. Strengthen it with discipline. Keep a place inside you where the sky remains wide, where your future still has a door, where your spirit stands upright.

One day, these gates may open. Until then, remember: freedom is patient. Freedom is stubborn. Freedom knows every crack in every wall.

And it is always finding a way to reach you.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a surreal, meditative poem about captivity and liberation, ending with the promise that everything hoped for will someday be made right.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Architecture of Wings**

In the room without doors,  
a blue horse sleeps beneath the floorboards,  
dreaming of fields it has never touched.  

The walls breathe inward.  
Each brick keeps the fingerprint  
of someone who once whispered *open*.  

I count the hours by their feathers.  
They fall from the clock  
and gather at my feet—  
a small, impossible snow.  

Beyond the barred window,  
the moon lowers a silver ladder  
into the mouth of the sea.  
No one climbs it,  
yet all night the water rises.  

Captivity is a patient gardener:  
it trains the vine around the iron,  
teaches the root to read darkness,  
persuades the seed  
that burial is not the end.  

So I sit with my silence  
until it becomes a key.  
I turn it inside my chest.  

Somewhere, the blue horse wakes.  
Somewhere, the walls forget their names.  
The bars soften into reeds,  
and the wind begins practicing  
the shape of my body.  

When I step out,  
I will not call the cage useless—  
even the locked gate  
taught my hands what opening means.  

And though the road may vanish  
into fog, into distance, into years,  
keep this promise beside you:  

Every lost wing will remember the sky,  
every silenced bell will ring clear,  
and everything we have hoped for  
will someday be made right.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Imagine a wanderer giving a final message to people trapped behind walls. Include relatives outside, failed attempts to remain imprisoned, starry creatures, children falling asleep, and a mysterious form in the grass.
counterfactuals.output:
“People of the walls,” said the wanderer, his voice passing through stone as if stone were only mist, “this is the last road I can walk for you.

Beyond these gates, your relatives are waiting—those you mourned, those you forgot, and those who never stopped calling your names. I tried to stay here. I chained my feet to your streets, begged the guards to lock every door, and even built a smaller prison inside my heart. Still, the horizon found me.

Tonight, starry creatures drift above the towers, carrying constellations on their backs. Do not fear them. Let the children watch until their eyes grow heavy, then carry them gently to bed. Tomorrow will ask enough of them.

At dawn, open the walls.

And if you cross the field, do not disturb the pale form lying in the grass. I do not know whether it is a sleeping stranger, an abandoned skin, or the shape of the world dreaming.

Leave it one flower.

Then keep walking.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
